sec: Precipitating triggers, West Haven staging and diagnostic tests

items.q: Match each category of precipitating factors in hepatic encephalopathy with its representative examples — 1) NH3-increasing nitrogenous loads 2) Alkalosis and electrolyte drivers … A) Hypokalemia from diuretics, hypovolemia, hyponatremia, and dehydration activating RAAS B) High dietary protein, constipation, GI hemorrhage, sepsis, and blood transfusion
items.exp: Direct NH3-increasing factors include high protein, constipation, GI hemorrhage, sepsis, and transfusion; alkalosis triggers include hypokalemia (diuretics), hypovolemia, hyponatremia, and dehydration. (Book p1011)

items.q: Why does metabolic alkalosis aggravate hepatic encephalopathy compared to acidosis?
opts: Alkalosis shifts the NH3 + H+ <-> NH4+ equilibrium toward uncharged NH3, facilitating non-ionic diffusion into the brain
Alkalosis irreversibly inhibits astrocytic glutamine synthetase
Alkalosis triggers rapid breakdown of hemoglobin into free iron
Alkalosis downregulates neuronal GABA-A receptor density
items.exp: In the equilibrium NH3 + H+ <-> NH4+, acidosis drives conversion to non-diffusible ammonium (NH4+), whereas alkalosis drives uncharged, diffusible NH3 into brain tissue. (Book p1011)

items.q: By which mechanism do sedative drugs precipitate or worsen hepatic encephalopathy?
opts: Inducing microvascular thrombosis in the portal vein
Blocking renal ammonium excretion in the collecting duct
items.exp: Under precipitating factors, sedatives (CNS drugs) act via '↑ GABA'. (Book p1011)

items.q: Match each category of hepatic encephalopathy under the West Haven Criteria with its included stages — 1) Covert HE 2) Overt HE … A) Grade-II, Grade-III, and Grade-IV B) Minimal HE and Grade-I
items.exp: West Haven criteria divide HE into Covert HE (minimal and Grade-I) and Overt HE (Grade-II, Grade-III, and Grade-IV). (Book p1011)

items.q: A 56-year-old cirrhotic patient appears completely normal on routine clinical bedside examination with no confusion or asterixis. However, formal psychometric testing demonstrates a positive Number Connection Test. What grade of hepatic encephalopathy is present?
items.exp: Minimal HE features a clinically normal patient whose deficit is revealed by psychometric testing, such as a positive Number Connection Test. (Book p1011)

items.q: Which of the following is NOT a feature of Grade-I hepatic encephalopathy under the West Haven Criteria?
items.exp: Grade-I features are Anxious, Altered Sleep Pattern, and Short attention span without asterixis; asterixis emerges in Grade-II. (Book p1011)

items.q: Match each West Haven Grade of Overt Hepatic Encephalopathy with its defining clinical features — 1) Grade-II 2) Grade-III 3) Grade-IV … A) Semi-stupor stage, gross disorientation, bizarre behavior, responsive to pain; rigidity, clonus, hyperreflexia B) Coma; decorticate posture, triphasic waves on EEG C) Personality issues, behavioral abnormalities, disorientation; mild slurring of speech, asterixis
items.exp: Grade-II = personality/behavior/disorientation + asterixis; Grade-III = semi-stupor/bizarre/pain-responsive + clonus/hyperreflexia; Grade-IV = coma + decorticate posture + triphasic EEG. (Book p1011)

items.q: At which West Haven grade does asterixis (flapping tremor) first become clinically demonstrable?
items.exp: Asterixis is absent in Minimal and Grade-I HE and first appears as a clinical finding in Grade-II. (Book p1011)

items.q: Fill up: In Grade-IV hepatic encephalopathy, motor posturing manifests as ______ posture, and electroencephalography reveals bilateral synchronous triphasic waves.
items.exp: Under Grade-IV clinical findings, the table lists 'Decorticate posture' and 'Triphasic EEG'. (Book p1011)

items.q: Assess the two statements on HE diagnostic signs: I Constructional apraxia in early encephalopathy is elicited by asking the patient to construct a star or matchstick pattern. II Triphasic waves on EEG are characteristically seen in Minimal hepatic encephalopathy.
items.exp: Statement I is true as shown in the star/matchstick test. Statement II is false because triphasic waves appear in Grade-IV coma. (Book p1011)

items.q: A 62-year-old man with alcoholic cirrhosis presents in a semi-stuporous state with gross disorientation and bizarre outbursts. He localizes and withdraws only to deep nailbed pressure. Physical examination reveals marked cogwheel rigidity, ankle clonus, and 3+ hyperreflexia. What is his West Haven grade?
items.exp: Semi-stupor, gross disorientation, response to pain, rigidity, clonus, and hyperreflexia define Grade-III hepatic encephalopathy. (Book p1011)
